1:
That a governor’s grief moved the city is the first thing noticed. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) has it noised abroad that their new governor, in whom they rejoiced, was himself in grief for them and their sin, so that a great congregation assembled to mingle their tears with his — and he draws the rule, that our weeping for other people’s sins may set those a weeping for themselves who would otherwise continue remorseless. When a man in authority under the king lamented the public corruptions so deeply, they concluded the corruptions were indeed grievous. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) adds that the account of his grief before the temple was dispersed over the city in an instant, and then repeats Henry’s own sentence about the happy influence the example of great ones may have upon their inferiors. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) reads the weeping as fear of a displeasure about to light on them.

Who Shechaniah was, and what it cost him to speak, is worked three ways. Clarke notes that he speaks for the people without acknowledging himself culpable, since his name is not in the list that follows, and takes him for a chief man whose support Ezra needed. Wesley finds the same absence from the catalogue but the presence there of his father Jehiel and five other sons of his grandfather Elam, and makes that the measure of the man: it was evidence of great courage that he durst so freely discharge his duty, honouring God above his nearest relations. Henry agrees he was not himself guilty — had he had the beam in his own eye he could not have seen so clearly to pluck it out of his brother’s — and guesses that his father’s strange wife may have been an unkind step-mother who made mischief in the family — if so, not the only time private resentments have been overruled by providence to serve the public good. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) dissent, holding that the Jehiel named later is not this man’s father at all.

On the hope offered, Henry is expansive and the others brief. Where else should there be hope but in Israel, he asks, since strangers to that commonwealth are said to have none? The case is sad but not desperate, the disease threatening but not incurable; now it is discovered it is half cured, and the valley of trouble is the door of hope, for the sin that truly troubles us shall not ruin us. From this he draws that in melancholy times we must observe what makes for us as well as against us, and that great saints must thankfully receive seasonable counsel from those much their inferiors, as Ezra did here. Clarke glosses the word as expectation of pardon, and John Gill (reformed) and Wesley both make the hope conditional on repentance and reformation.

On the remedy itself Henry both urges it and refuses to let it stand as a precedent. What has been done amiss must be undone as far as possible, and nothing less is true repentance: sin must have a bill of divorce given it, though it be dear as the wife of one’s bosom, nay as a right eye. But Shechaniah’s counsel, he says plainly, will not hold now. Marriages with unbelievers are certainly sinful and ought not to be made, yet they are not null — what ought not to have been done must, being done, abide — and the gospel rule is that if a brother has an unbelieving wife pleased to dwell with him, let him not put her away. Wesley attends to the children, cast out of the commonwealth of Israel but not utterly forsaken, provision being probably made for them by authority. Keil and Delitzsch add that Ezra had remained on his knees throughout the speech before rising to swear them.
6:
The penalty attached to the summons is construed alike by three voices. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) notes that Ezra, authorised by the king to enforce his orders with penalties, threatened forfeiture and outlawry: the doom of a man who would not attend was that his substance should in his stead be for ever appropriated to the service of their religion, while he himself was for ever excluded from its privileges. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) make the legal point exactly: the forfeiture is not destruction of the goods, as the law prescribed for a city fallen into idolatry, but their appropriation to the temple on the analogy of another statute. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) reaches the same reading and finds the Greek version already there, rendering it that all his substance shall be devoted to a holy use, the man himself excommunicated and exiled from Israel. John Gill (reformed) accounts for the shortness of the notice: three days was fixed for quick dispatch, to forestall any scheme to obstruct the business, and lest those who had agreed should repent and go from their word.

The rain is read as a sign, and Henry reads it two ways at once. It was a token of God’s displeasure, which perhaps kept some away and was grievous to those who met in the open street; yet when they wept the heavens wept too, signifying that though God was angry at their sin he was well pleased with their repentance. And it was besides an indication of the good fruits of that repentance, since rain makes the earth fruitful. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) keeps only the first half, that they took it for a token of displeasure against them. Clarke declines the sign and gives the season: the ninth month answers to part of our December, the coldest and most rainy part of the year in Palestine, and the Greek renders the clause simply because of the winter.

That the business was handed to a commission rather than settled on the spot is approved by all; Henry gives the reasons. It could not be done then, for the thing was not yet put into a method and the people could not stand out in the rain; the delinquents were many and would take time to examine; and nice cases would arise that could not be adjudged without debate. Take time, he has them say, and we shall have done the sooner; do it in a hurry and we shall do it by halves. He adds what he plainly admires, that Ezra let his zeal be guided by the people’s prudence and was not ashamed to own the advice came from them. Keil and Delitzsch put the same necessity administratively: the cases being too many for one hearing, the rulers as judicial authorities must decide, and the offenders in every city appear before them. Wesley and Gill both read the proposal as the settling of the great council at Jerusalem, Wesley adding that the local judges were joined to it as best able to inform it of the persons and the facts.

Clarke alone looks past the decision to what it cost, and whether it held. The dismissal was a great hardship on women and children who did not know the law that made such marriages void; yet he will not have them turned away desolate, taking it for granted that each received a portion according to her husband’s circumstances, since humanity must have dictated it and no law of God is contrary to humanity. Then he raises the doubt no one else raises: there is some room to question whether they did put them finally away, for years later Nehemiah found Jews who had married wives of Ashdod, Ammon and Moab — and if those were not the same women, the same offence was simply being continued.
15:
Whether the two men named were employed in the business or stood against it divides the voices, and the Hebrew bears either. John Gill (reformed) takes them as employed, to see the affair conducted as proposed, each city’s magistrates bringing the delinquents in turn. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) reads it the same way and fills out the office: they were to see each city’s officers and offenders come in order, keep account of the names dispatched, and prepare the business for the judges; and he makes these two priests and their helpers Levites, to inform the parties in any matter of doubt. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) take the contrary sense, that the two opposed the proposal and were backed by two Levites without being able to carry it; they read the opening particle as a qualification of the assembly’s agreement, cite Lightfoot and a rabbinic authority for the construction, and set against them the Vulgate and one explanation they call decidedly incorrect. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) gives the employed sense first, guessing these were the men who had made the proposal and so the fittest to pursue it, but then reports Lightfoot’s contrary reading, grants the original will very well bear it, and adds that it would be strange if a work of this kind met with no opposition at all.

On the commission Henry is both admiring and precise. Ezra presided, with chief men of the fathers qualified with wisdom and zeal above others; it was happy for them that they had such a man to head them, since they could not have done it well without his direction, though he would not do it without their concurrence. They began on the first day of the tenth month, ten days after the method was proposed, and finished in three; they must have sat closely, or could never have despatched so many causes in the time. And Henry adds the qualification that makes the delay intelligible: everyone impeached was presumably asked what cause he could show against being parted, and, judging by other cases, a wife proselyted to the Jewish religion was not to be put away — a trial requiring great care. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) counts the same three whole months, and Wesley notes that the commissioners sequestered themselves from all other business and gave themselves wholly to this.

That priests were among the guilty is pressed by two. Henry notes that many of them, and even of the high priest’s family, were found in the trespass, though the law had particularly provided for the honour of their marriages, that being holy themselves they should not marry such as were profane; those who should have taught others the law broke it themselves, and by their example emboldened others. Gill makes the inference the other way about: it need not be wondered at that the evil spread among the people when those who understood the law, and should have taught it, set such an example. Keil and Delitzsch supply the genealogy, that the four named first were sons and brethren of the high priest Jeshua and, by the earlier roll, distant cousins of his.

How they bound themselves is reported three ways. Keil and Delitzsch take the phrase literally, that they bound themselves by shaking hands to dismiss the wives and sever them from the congregation, the following word condemning them to bring a ram for their trespass. Clarke has them bind themselves in the most solemn manner, as the other delinquents had, acknowledging their iniquity by each offering a ram. Henry has them promise under their hand, and reports that some think the oath was made with hands lifted up; and he names the law behind the ram, the offering appointed for a trespass, so that in bringing it they owned both their guilt and its desert.
24:
With the singers and porters the clerical part of the roll closes, and three voices mark the turn. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) count one singer and three porters here, which brings the Levites to ten in all, and refer both orders back to the roll of those who had returned from exile, where the same two classes are enumerated. They then read the phrase that follows as the heading of a new class: of Israel means the laity, as distinguished from priests and Levites. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) says the same after Calmet, that these are simple Israelites, set apart from the priests, Levites and singers already named; and John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) glosses it as the people of Israel, distinguished from the orders hitherto listed.

Keil and Delitzsch alone look at the laity’s roll as a document and find it damaged. Eighty-six names are given in it, belonging to ten families of those who had returned with Zerubbabel, each of which they identify against their own survey of those families; and one name in the list they would read differently, on the authority of the written text against the vowels supplied for it. But the real difficulty is that the sons of Bani are named twice over in the one list, which they call strange and judge to be a copyist’s error rather than a fact: one of the two headings must stand for some other family, and Bertheau’s conjecture is that a different name had once stood in its place. They locate the fault in the second occurrence, and argue it from the arithmetic rather than from the spelling. Every other family in the roll contributes four, six, seven or eight men; after the second heading no fewer than twenty-seven names follow. That is too many to have belonged to one family, so the error cannot be the mere mistranscription of a single word — a whole block of names has been gathered under a heading that does not belong to them, and the damage is to the structure of the roll rather than to its spelling.
44:
The closing notice that some of these men had children by their foreign wives is read as evidence of how few did. John Gill (reformed) puts the whole number of offenders at about a hundred and thirteen. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) infers that most of the wives were barren, and reads that barrenness as providence: it manifested God’s displeasure against such matches, and it kept the putting away from being encumbered with too many difficulties. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) draws the opposite emphasis from the same clause, that only a few had children but also that the law was put in execution rigorously, children notwithstanding.

Wesley then closes the chapter where its reformers could not. One would think the grievance altogether removed, yet it is met with again in Nehemiah; such corruptions are easily and insensibly brought in, though not easily purged out, and the best reformers can but do their endeavour. It is only the Redeemer himself who, when he comes to Zion, will effectually turn away ungodliness from Jacob.

Clarke ends on a textual curiosity no other voice raises. He reports from Justin Martyr’s dialogue with Trypho that Ezra offered a paschal lamb on this occasion and addressed the people in words that are not in any text we have: that this passover is our Savior and our Refuge, that if they would be persuaded of it and let it enter their hearts, humbling themselves to him in a sign and afterwards believing in him, the place should not be destroyed for ever; but that if they would not believe nor hearken to his preaching, they should be a laughing-stock to the Gentiles. Justin’s claim, which Clarke relays without endorsing, is that the Jews blotted this passage out of the book of Ezra from enmity to Christ, and that they cancelled several other places in the same spirit. Clarke adds the plainer bibliographical note that in the Hebrew this book and the next make only one, that the Masoretic enumeration of sections treats them as conjoined, and that Nehemiah is nonetheless sometimes distinguished as a second book of Esdras; and he signs the place off with the date of his own correction.
